5:## 0. How to read this
44:## 1. Parsing and the syntax tree
110:## 2. Name resolution and grammar expansion
189:## 3. The checker
336:## 4. Desugaring, overload rewriting, and the switches
427:## 5. Code generation
498:## 6. The run: the second JVM and the class loader
581:## 7. Native bindings in both worlds
639:## 8. `nat`: a size in a type
820:## 9. Glossary

189	## 3. The checker
190	
191	### What it is, and when it runs
192	
193	The type checker is written in Scala and lives under `scala_src/`: 59 files,
194	19,419 lines in nine subpackages (`modules-and-phases.md` A.2). The parts that
195	matter here, measured at HEAD: `typechecker/` 6,388 lines (the driver
196	`STypeChecker.scala`, 612, plus the standalone checkers beside it),
197	`typechecker/impls/` 3,086 (the cases, split five ways), `types/` 1,688 (the
198	subtype lattice, `TypeAnalyzer.scala` 799), `useful/` 3,438 (helpers, of which
199	`STypesUtil.scala` is 1,961), `typechecker/staticenv/` 682, `overloading/` 540,
200	`linker/` 494.
201	
202	It runs only on the compile path. The TYPECHECK phase is in the interpreter's
203	phase list too (`phases/PhaseOrder.java:130`), but the property
204	`fortress.compile.typecheck` defaults to false (`Shell.java:1275`) and
205	`StaticChecker.checkCompilationUnit` returns the tree untouched when the flag
206	is off (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:163-166`). `walk` additionally calls
207	`setScala(false)` (`Shell.java:421-422`), which reaches an `Error` saying the
208	Java checker is gone if checking is ever switched on that way
209	(`StaticChecker.java:228-229`). There is no command-line switch that makes the
210	interpreter type-check (FACTS, execution model).
211	
212	### What runs around it
213	
214	`TypeCheckPhase` builds the index objects for apis and components, checks the
215	apis, then the components (`phases/TypeCheckPhase.java:32-58`). For one
216	component `StaticChecker` runs, in order: an api type extractor, a type
217	normalizer, a trait table and a `TypeAnalyzer`, a `Thunker` that gives elided
218	return types thunks, then `STypeChecker.typeCheck`, then well-formedness again,
219	the overloading rules, export checking and the variance checker
220	(`StaticChecker.java:196-290`). One of those is switched by path: the variance
221	checker is skipped when the compiled-expression desugaring is off, with the
222	comment "Hack: don't run the variance checker if running the interpreter"
223	(`StaticChecker.java:288-290`).
224	
225	### How it walks the tree
226	
227	`STypeChecker` is an abstract class with two abstract methods: `check(node)`
228	and `checkExpr(expr, expected)` (`typechecker/STypeChecker.scala:403, 419`).
229	The second takes an *expected type* — the checker is bidirectional: it can push
230	a type down into an expression as well as read one out, and that expected type
231	is what drives inference (`:405-417`).
232	
233	The implementation is mixed in as five traits, and the routing is one pattern
234	match: a `Component`, `TraitDecl`, `ObjectDecl`, `FnDecl` or `VarDecl` goes to
235	`Decls`; a function application, `case`, `fn` expression, functional reference,
236	method invocation, operator application or subscript goes to `Functionals`; an
237	assignment, chained comparison, juxtaposition or `MathPrimary` goes to
238	`Operators`; an `Op` or `Link` also to `Operators`; everything else to `Misc`
239	(`typechecker/impls/Dispatch.scala:59-99`).
240	
241	`typeCheck` is the only entry external code may call, and it swallows a
242	`ProgramError` into the error list rather than propagating it
243	(`STypeChecker.scala:430-440`). Note what it does *not* catch: a `NotYetImple-
244	mented` error or a `ClassCastException` is not a `ProgramError`, and takes the
245	whole compile down. That distinction is the whole of section 8's problem.
246	
247	### What it writes onto the tree
248	
249	A type, per expression, and nothing else. `SExprUtil.addType` returns the same
250	expression with the type inserted into its `ExprInfo`
251	(`scala_src/useful/SExprUtil.scala:60-77`); `getType` reads it back
252	(`:31`). No new representation is produced, which is why the same `nodes/` tree
253	continues into desugaring and code generation
254	(`modules-and-phases.md` B.6).
255	
256	One more thing is recorded and easy to miss: at a call site the checker chooses
257	a candidate and records the static arguments it settled on, on the reference
258	node, for the code generator to mangle into a name later
259	(`nat-checking-plan.md` §b step 12; `compiler/NamingCzar.java:1888-1910`).
260	
261	### How mature it is, in today's counts
262	
263	The measurement is the interpreter's own library — 4,507 lines, 446 top-level
264	declarations — pushed through the compile path with the checker's failures
265	caught per declaration (`perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen.md` §2.3, §5.1):
266	
267	| | count |
268	|---|---|
269	| checked with no error of its own | 237 |
270	| checked, errors reported on it | 97 |
271	| **crashed the checker** | **112** |
272	
273	The 112 crashes: 81 at `STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` (the `nat`/`int`/`bool`
274	kinds), 29 `ClassCastException: TraitType cannot be cast to IntExpr` at
275	`NodeUpdateVisitor.forIntArg:5310` (a size written out as a static argument),
276	1 "Type is not inferred", 1 "Not in the trait table"
277	(`desugar-codegen.md` §5.1).
278	
279	Three further facts from the same measurement. The prelude apis raise 960
280	errors, 257 distinct, of which **712 are one rewrite's doing** — the compile
281	path's own `extends Object` pre-desugaring, section 4 (`desugar-codegen.md`
282	§4.3). Overload dispatch generation, which consumes the checker's results, ran
283	**1,046 seconds on this library without emitting a single declaration** and was
284	stopped by hand (`desugar-codegen.md` §3 caveat 3). And of the code
285	generator's 313 refusals, only **5** are on declarations the checker had
286	checked clean (§5.1) — so the distance between the interpreter's library and
287	bytecode is the checker, not the back end (`desugar-codegen.md` §6).
288	
289	### What it refuses or has never implemented
290	
291	- **Non-type static parameters.** `makeInferenceArg` is `NI.nyi()` for
292	  `KindInt`, `KindBool`, `KindDim`, `KindUnit` and `KindNat`
293	  (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:546-559`). Section 8.
294	- **Equality of two sizes.** `pEqv(IntArg, IntArg)` returns `pTrue()` under the
295	  comment "Not handling all static args properly yet"
296	  (`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:327-337`): today any two sizes are
297	  equal. Exclusion has the matching hole, "Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args"
298	  (`:445-451`).
299	- **Export checking of sizes.** `ExportChecker.equalIntExprs` is `= false` with
300	  the comment "Not implemented!" (`typechecker/ExportChecker.scala:648`).
301	- **Non-type where-clause bindings.** `NI.nyi("non-type where clause
302	  bindings")` (`typechecker/staticenv/KindEnv.scala:126`); type bindings are
303	  handled (`spec-to-implementation.md` chapter 12 row).
304	- **Type aliases.** `IndexBuilder` calls `bug("Not yet implemented")`
305	  (`scala_src/typechecker/IndexBuilder.scala:187`) — and `IndexBuilder` runs on
306	  both paths, so this one is not compile-path-only
307	  (`spec-to-implementation.md` chapter 6 row).
308	- **Templates.** There is no `TemplateGap` or `_SyntaxTransformation` case
309	  anywhere under `scala_src/typechecker/`, so a program using a user grammar
310	  cannot be checked as written (FACTS, a user grammar on the compile path).
311	
312	### How it differs from the interpreter's run-time dispatch
313	
314	The interpreter never consults a static type. An overloaded name is resolved
315	per call, on the run-time values, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatch`
316	(`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:787`); a failure reads
317	"Failed to find any matching overload" (`:795`). The compile path instead
318	generates one dispatch method per overloaded name that tests argument types
319	from most to least specific (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1944, 1964`), and the
320	candidate lists the two start from are different: the interpreter's come from
321	the disambiguator, the compiler's from the checker
322	(`modules-and-phases.md` B.7).
323	
324	The practical consequence, measured: a function declared on a sized subtype and
325	applied to a value whose *static* type is the unsized supertype is refused by
326	the checker and runs on the interpreter. Probe `p3_static_dispatch.fss`:
327	compile path, `(Vec[\RR64\], Vec[\RR64\])->RR64 is not applicable to an
328	argument of type (Arr[\RR64\], Arr[\RR64\])`; interpreter, prints its answer
329	(`compiler-probes/array-design-review/p3_static_dispatch.compile.out`,
330	`.interp.out`). This is how the target program is written throughout, and it is
331	the first thing a `nat` fix does *not* repair (`array-design-review.md`
332	finding 1).
333	
334	---
335	
336	## 4. Desugaring, overload rewriting, and the switches
337	
338	### Three desugarings, split by what must be known

639	## 8. `nat`: a size in a type
640	
641	### What the specification says it is
642	
643	A `nat` static parameter is the keyword `nat` followed by an identifier, in the
644	same white brackets as a type parameter
645	(`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:68-81`). Three sentences fix its
646	meaning. "These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values"
647	(`:82`) — so a size is not erased. A `nat` parameter "may be used to
648	instantiate other `nat` parameters, or to appear in any context that a variable
649	of type `N32` can appear, except that it cannot be assigned to" (`:83-86`) — so
650	in value position it is a read-only number, and in type position it may only
651	instantiate other sizes. And the chapter's single example is exactly an array
652	shape: `makeVector[\T extends Number, nat s0\](): Vector[\T,s0\]`
653	(`:94-97`), one symbol occurring in the parameter list and in the return type,
654	which must agree.
655	
656	The chapter opens with its own status note: "Non-type static parameters and
657	static expressions are not yet supported. The examples in this chapter are not
658	tested nor run by the interpreter." (`:15-17`). So the gap is not a regression;
659	the team shipped the specification saying so (`nat-checking-plan.md` §a).
660	
661	Sizes were meant to check shapes, not to optimize anything: the spec builds no
662	optimization on them anywhere (FACTS, execution model). The one recorded
663	implementation stance in the team's own internal appendix is "don't
664	instantiate" — the checker treats a size as opaque, two different literals are
665	different types, and arithmetic on sizes is not something the checker reasons
666	about (`nat-checking-plan.md` §a, from
667	`Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex:182, 206`).
668	
669	### Where sizes actually occur
670	
671	The interpreter's library has 81 declarations with `nat`/`int`/`bool`
672	parameters; the target program's array vocabularies have 30 and 27; the
673	compiler's own prelude has exactly **one**, and it is empty:
674	`trait Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\] extends Object end`
675	(`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:512`; census in `nat-checking-plan.md` §d). In
676	every one of them the arguments are symbols and literals; the census found no
677	arithmetic inside white brackets in the library or either vocabulary
678	(`nat-checking-plan.md` §d) — with three exceptions in storing objects that a
679	later review found (`array-design-review.md` finding 5), which matters if the
680	rule adopted is "refuse arithmetic".
681	
682	That the compiler prelude has one empty `nat` declaration is the shape of the
683	whole problem: the compiler's library is written to stay inside what the
684	checker can do (`spec-to-implementation.md` §4.3; FACTS, ledger 307).
685	
686	### What the checker lacks, in three parts
687	
688	**Representation.** There is no inference variable for a size. When the checker
689	needs to infer static arguments at a call, it makes one fresh variable per
690	static parameter; for a type parameter that is `TypeArg(_InferenceVarType)` and
691	for an operator parameter `OpArg(_InferenceVarOp)`, and for `KindNat`,
692	`KindInt`, `KindBool`, `KindDim` and `KindUnit` it is `NI.nyi()`
693	(`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:546-559`). That call is reached from
694	ordinary call-site inference and from the overloading checker alike, which is
695	why the crash appears twice when a library is checked
696	(`nat-checking-plan.md` §b). Two representations are on the table: a new AST
697	node `_InferenceVarInt` beside the existing two, which is symmetric but
698	regenerates every visitor class; or an `IntRef` with a reserved name, which
699	needs no AST change and can therefore be prototyped under a classpath shadow
700	(`nat-checking-plan.md` §c, "Representation").
701	
702	**Equality.** Two sizes are compared in exactly one place, and today it says
703	yes to everything: `case (_: IntArg, _: IntArg) => pTrue()`, under the comment
704	"Not handling all static args properly yet"
705	(`scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:332`). Exclusion has the twin hole
706	(`:445-451`), and the export checker's `equalIntExprs` is `= false`
707	(`typechecker/ExportChecker.scala:648`). The rule the plan proposes is the
708	interpreter's own: a literal must equal a literal, a symbol equals itself, a
709	symbol is not a literal, and an inference variable takes an equality constraint
710	— which is a port of `IntNat.unifyStaticArg`
711	(`interpreter/evaluator/types/IntNat.java:127-147`;
712	`nat-checking-plan.md` §c, "Rules").
713	
714	**Inference.** The constraint solver has two tracks, types and operators: `And`
715	carries a map per type variable and a map per operator variable
716	(`scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:50`), and `solve` returns a pair of
717	substitutions (`:420-460`). A size needs a third track, unified as the operator
718	track is, by cliques with structural equality
719	(`nat-checking-plan.md` §c, §"What it touches"). One more hole travels with it:
720	`hasInferenceVars` looks only for type variables
721	(`STypesUtil.scala:778-789`), so an unsolved size would leak silently into a
722	generated name instead of producing "not enough context".
723	
724	**Size of the change, and the caveat on it.** About 24 functions in five Scala
725	files, 200-300 lines, most of it the mechanical third track in `Formula.scala`;
726	no catalogued test flips; five compiler tests must stay green
727	(`nat-checking-plan.md` §d). The caveat: the plan's "no Java" is unproven — one
728	of the two known crashes has Java frames, in the static-type replacer, and six
729	Java files in `compiler/` handle `IntArg`
730	(`array-design-review.md` finding 6). The instrument that settles it is a
731	shadow session (edited copies compiled and put first on the class path), which
732	has been done once before for a checker plan and gated green
733	(FACTS, the template-checking fix), and has not been done for this one
734	(`array-design-review.md` §1b).
735	
736	### What the loader and the code generator lack
737	
738	Section 6 in one paragraph: the size is mangled into the instantiation name
739	(`NamingCzar.java:1826-1832`, `:1888-1910`) and nothing reads it back — the
740	runtime consults only the operator kind (`Naming.java:95-108`), the generic
741	RTTI class has no size field (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:1600-1622`), a
742	size in an `extends` clause is refused outright
743	(`CodeGen.java:5793`), and a size in value position compiles to a reference the
744	loader cannot satisfy (`array-design-review.md` §1b, probe 6). So the first
745	sized object that compiles will need work in Java after the checker work in
746	Scala; the review counts at least three gated batches where the design counted
747	two (`array-design-review.md` finding 6).
748	
749	### The thing a `nat` fix does not fix
750	
751	The target program's values carry their sizes at run time and not in their
752	static types: `array[\E\](n)` reflects `n` into a size and returns the *unsized*
753	`Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]`, and the interpreter then dispatches on the run-time
754	object. On the compile path the static type is what is consulted, so the
755	applications fail even with no `nat` in sight — probe `p3_static_dispatch`
756	above (`array-design-review.md` finding 1). Teaching the checker sizes makes
757	sized *declarations* checkable; making the model's *applications* check is a
758	separate decision about how the model is typed.
759	
760	### Four precedents, and what each would mean here
761	
762	These four are background from outside this tree — nothing in the repository
763	documents them — offered because each one already took a decision that is now
764	in front of us. The in-tree consequence after each is cited.
765	
766	**Dependent ML.** Xi and Pfenning's design indexes types by a separate, decidable
767	domain of integers, with constraints solved by an arithmetic solver, precisely
768	so that dependent types do not drag full term evaluation into type checking.
769	Here it names the boundary question: whether sizes live in a small language of
770	their own with a solver behind them, or stay symbols and literals compared by
771	equality — which is what the plan proposes and what the team's own "don't
772	instantiate" stance implies (`nat-checking-plan.md` §a, §c).
773	
774	**X10's constrained types.** X10 attaches boolean constraints to types —
775	`Array[T]{rank==2}` — and discharges them with a pluggable constraint solver,
776	which buys array-shape checking at the cost of a solver in the compiler and a
777	constraint language in the surface syntax. Here it is the shape of the *next*
778	step past equality, and the reason to take equality first: Fortress already has
779	the syntax for it, a where clause with an `IntConstraint`
780	(`ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast:1485-1496`), and the checker ignores
781	where clauses entirely (`STypesUtil.scala:625`;
782	`typechecker/staticenv/KindEnv.scala:126`).
783	
784	**Haskell's type-level naturals.** `GHC.TypeLits` gives a kind of naturals with
785	literals and type-level arithmetic that the compiler solves only for closed
786	literals — real algebra needs a normalizing solver supplied as a plugin — plus
787	a `KnownNat` dictionary to read a size back as a value. Here the second half
788	already exists (`LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi` reflects a size to a number),
789	and the first half is the honest price of arithmetic in types, which is why the
790	plan draws its line at symbols and literals and refuses `Vector[\T, n+1\]` as
791	ill-formed rather than promising to check it (`nat-checking-plan.md` §c, §g).
792	
793	**C++ non-type template parameters.** `template<size_t N>` instantiates a
794	distinct class per value, equality of sizes is syntactic identity after
795	constant folding, and the size is a compile-time constant with no run-time
796	representation at all. Here it is the contrast that matters most: Fortress
797	sizes are "instantiated at runtime with numeric values"
798	(`trait-parameters.tex:82`), the interpreter really does evaluate `+`, `-` and
799	`*` on them while instantiating
800	(`interpreter/evaluator/EvalType.java:431-464`), and the class loader stamps by
801	name only (section 6) — so C++'s per-value specialization is *not* what this
802	loader does, and any plan that assumes a size disappears at compile time is
803	assuming the wrong runtime.
804	
805	### What is a decision, not a fact
806	
807	Four things the record leaves to Pavol, each already stated in a report:
808	whether the inference variable is a new AST node or a reserved name
809	(`nat-checking-plan.md` §c); what an unconstrained size does — default to 0, or
810	be an error at first use as the interpreter does, with the six library
811	declarations that carry dead sizes as the test case
812	(`nat-checking-plan.md` §c; `array-design-review.md` finding 7); whether
813	arithmetic inside white brackets is refused as ill-formed, which three library
814	storing objects would then fail (`array-design-review.md` finding 5); and
815	whether the checker rung is scheduled before or after a shadow session has
816	shown where the crash actually lives (`array-design-review.md` §1b).
817

336	## 4. Desugaring, overload rewriting, and the switches
337	
338	### Three desugarings, split by what must be known
339	
340	The split is by information, not by path (`modules-and-phases.md` B.5).
341	PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR must precede name binding because it introduces names.
342	PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR produces code that must itself be checked. DESUGAR runs
343	*after* checking because getter/setter and coercion rewriting need types
344	(`compiler/Desugarer.java:36-45`). `Desugarer.desugarApi` is a no-op: an api
345	comes out unchanged (`Desugarer.java:82-85`).
346	
347	### The switches, which are what make the two paths differ
348	
349	Which visitors run is decided by flags on `Shell`, not by the phase list. The
350	two world-setters are eight lines each:
351	
352	- `useCompilerLibraries()` sets the `extends Object` pre-desugaring **on** and
353	  assignment desugaring on (`Shell.java:371-377`).
354	- `useInterpreterLibraries()` sets the `extends Object` pre-desugaring off and
355	  the compiled-expression desugaring **off** (`Shell.java:379-386`).
356	
357	Three further getters are gated on `use_scala`, which `walk` turns off
358	(`Shell.java:421-422`): coercion desugaring (`Shell.java:280-282`), chained
359	comparison (`:284-286`) and compound/tuple assignment with subscript rewriting
360	(`:268-270`). The defaults themselves are one block of fields
361	(`Shell.java:1273-1286`).
362	
363	Read as a table, for the four desugarings that differ:
364	
365	| desugaring | interpreter | compile path | site |
366	|---|---|---|---|
367	| `extends Object` on unbounded static parameters | off | **on** | `PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:134-148` |
368	| case expressions, type ascription | off | on | `Desugarer.java:123-127`, `:140-144` |
369	| typecase, bodyless-`FnDecl`-to-abstract | off | on | `PreTypeCheckDesugarer.java:117-126` |
370	| coercion, chained comparison, assignment/subscript | off (`use_scala` false) | on | `Shell.java:268-270, 280-286` |
371	
372	Coercion is the sharpest of these: the compile path has coercion and the
373	interpreter has none at all — no `Coercion` or `coerce` anywhere under
374	`interpreter/` (`spec-to-implementation.md` §4.1, coercion row).
375	
376	### The `extends Object` rewrite, and why it is on this page
377	
378	When the switch is on, every unbounded static parameter is given an
379	`extends Object` bound (`PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:134-148`).
380	The checker then rejects every instantiation of such a parameter **at a tuple
381	type**, because a tuple type is not a subtype of `Object` in this checker:
382	`Ill-formed type: Condition[\()\]`, `Generator[\(T,U)\]`, and so on. On the
383	interpreter's library that is 712 of the 960 prelude-api errors and 618 of the
384	1,204 component errors — larger than the 93 tower errors already on record
385	(`desugar-codegen.md` §4.3). It costs no code-generation failure, because
386	nothing gets that far.
387	
388	This is a decision point, not a bug report: the rewrite exists for the compiler
389	world's own benefit, and the largest single obstacle between one library text
390	and the compile path is this switch rather than anything in the library.
391	
392	### DESUGAR itself
393	
394	Case expressions, coercions, getters and setters, type ascription
395	(`Desugarer.java:114-147`). Measured on the interpreter's library: DESUGAR and
396	OVERLOADREWRITE together report **zero diagnostics** on all 4,507 lines
397	(`desugar-codegen.md` §4.2). Whatever is wrong between that library and the
398	compile path, it is not the desugaring.
399	
400	### OVERLOADREWRITE
401	
402	A reference with several candidates is replaced by a reference to one synthetic
403	name spelled `f{f1,f2,…}`, and a `_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` declaring it is
404	appended to the component (`compiler/OverloadRewriter.java:66-92`). The same
405	class runs on both paths with a flag: `forInterpreter=false` on the compile
406	path, `true` on the other, and the flag decides which of the disambiguator's
407	two candidate lists is read (`OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:107`).
408	
409	Downstream, the interpreter turns that declaration into an
410	`OverloadedFunction` that searches at run time, and the code generator hands it
411	to `OverloadSet`, which emits a decision tree (`modules-and-phases.md` B.7).
412	On the interpreter's library, 100 of the code generator's 313 refusals are on
413	these synthesized declarations, and that figure is a floor, because dispatch
414	generation had to be switched off to finish the measurement at all
415	(`desugar-codegen.md` §3 caveat 3, §5.1).
416	
417	### The interpreter's own tail, for contrast
418	
419	After its phase chain the interpreter runs one more rewrite the compiler has no
420	counterpart for: every variable, function and operator reference is annotated
421	with its lexical nesting depth, and the result is cached
422	(`interpreter/env/ComponentWrapper.java:109-114`;
423	`interpreter/rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java:61-85`).
424	
425	---
426	
427	## 5. Code generation
428	
429	**What runs.** `CodeGenerationPhase` runs three analyses per component — free
430	variables, free-variable types, and a parallelism analysis — and then `CodeGen`
431	(`phases/CodeGenerationPhase.java:183-196`).
432	
433	**What `CodeGen` is.** One Java file, 6,819 lines, a visitor over the AST
434	(`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:199`) with 45 `public void for…` methods, two
435	of them helpers, so about 43 node kinds have a case (counted at HEAD).
436	Anything with no `forX` method reaches `defaultCase`, which throws
437	`Can't compile <node>` (`CodeGen.java:1668-1670`, `sayWhat` at `:1551-1553`).
438	So "absent on the compile path" usually means "no visitor"
439	(`spec-to-implementation.md` §2, codegen column).
440	
441	**Where the output goes.** The constructor opens the jar immediately —
442	`bytecode_cache/<dotted component name>.jar`
443	(`CodeGen.java:392-394`, the cache path from `compiler/NamingCzar.java:132`) —
444	which is why a failed compile leaves a truncated or zero-byte jar behind
445	(FACTS, execution model). There is no link step producing a single artifact:
446	`compile` leaves jars and `run` finds them by class path
447	(`modules-and-phases.md` B.9).
448	
449	**How types are lowered.** Every Fortress type becomes a JVM reference type:
450	traits become interfaces, `RR64` becomes the runtime class `FRR64`, and there
451	is no `dadd` or `dmul` anywhere in a generated loop — arrays are library
452	objects over `get`/`put`, not `double[]`
453	(`repo-internals.md:129`; FACTS, execution model, with the bytecode in
454	`perf-probes/boxing/javap/`). Classes are written with ASM using
455	`COMPUTE_FRAMES` (`CodeGen.java:406`), at classfile version 1.6, because the
456	load-time rewriting of section 6 does not maintain stack-map frames
457	(`repo-internals.md:129`).
458	
459	**Generic declarations are emitted once.** A generic trait, object or function
460	is compiled to a *template* class; the instances are produced later, at class
461	load (`modules-and-phases.md` B.9, B.11). Section 6.
462	
463	**What it refuses, deliberately.** Four places compute a boolean called
464	`canCompile` and throw if it is false:
465	
466	| site | requires |
467	|---|---|
468	| `FnDecl` (`CodeGen.java:2948-2957`) | no where clause, no contract, no unhandled modifiers, **not inside a block** — so no local functions |
469	| `ObjectDecl` (`:4086-4097`) | no where clause, no throws clause, no contract |
470	| `TraitDecl` (`:4997-5006`) | the same three |
471	| `SubscriptExpr` (`:4939-4940`) | no static arguments, an operator present, the object a plain `VarRef` |
472	
473	Where clauses are therefore refused outright on all three declaration forms
474	(`:2949`, `:4089`, `:5000`), and a local function is refused with
475	`Can't compile LetFn` (FACTS, execution model; ledger 304). A `throws` clause
476	on a function has been accepted since 2011 by a comment in the code, but is
477	still refused on traits and objects (`:4089`, `:5000`;
478	`spec-to-implementation.md` chapter 14 row).
479	
480	**What it refuses by omission**, on the features the target program uses:
481	`label`/`exit`, `spawn`, array literals (`ArrayElements`), array
482	comprehensions, and `atomic` in expression position all have no `forX` method
483	(`spec-to-implementation.md` chapters 5 and 13 rows).
484	
485	**What it did on the interpreter's library**, once the checker was stepped
486	around (`desugar-codegen.md` §5.1): 275 declarations emitted, 313 refused. Of
487	the 313, 227 lacked a type annotation, 55 had no visitor (`Juxt` 53, `Label` 1,
488	`AmbiguousMultifixOpExpr` 1), 14 were a `nat` static argument, 7 a malformed
489	overload set, 6 a type-reference or RTTI limit, 2 a kind-environment failure,
490	2 other. `canCompile` refused **nothing** in this library, and no native
491	binding was missing. And of all 313, only five were on a declaration the
492	checker had checked clean: four of them a number where a type was expected
493	(`nat s0` in a parameter list, `Rank[\1\]` in an extends clause), one a method
494	call on an intersection-typed receiver (`desugar-codegen.md` §5.1, "The five").
495

110	## 2. Name resolution and grammar expansion
111	
112	Four phases run before the checker, in this order:
113	PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR
114	(`phases/PhaseOrder.java:137-141`). They are identical on both paths except for
115	switches, which section 4 takes up.
116	
117	**PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR.** A rewrite that must happen before names are bound,
118	because it introduces calls to names: `extends Object` made explicit,
119	conditional operators (`AND:`, `OR:`) turned into thunks, reductions made
120	explicit (`desugarer/PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:39-52`). One of
121	its rewrites is compile-path-only and expensive; section 4 returns to it.
122	
123	**DISAMBIGUATE is where a name becomes a declaration.** `Disambiguator` runs
124	four visitors in order: `SelfParamDisambiguator`, `TypeDisambiguator`,
125	`NonterminalDisambiguator` (apis only) and the Scala `ExprDisambiguator`
126	(`compiler/Disambiguator.java:90, 145, 153, 185, 300, 308, 362`). After this
127	phase every name is fully qualified, and nothing downstream re-resolves names
128	(`modules-and-phases.md` B.4).
129	
130	**Two things it decides that matter later.** First, a bare name that could be a
131	function becomes an `FnRef` carrying a *candidate set* — every function of that
132	name in scope — and it carries two such lists: the interpreter's, which is all
133	matching names, and the "new" one, which is the unambiguous names that the type
134	checker will narrow (`modules-and-phases.md` B.4;
135	`compiler/desugarer/OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:107`). The two paths later read
136	different lists (section 4).
137	
138	Second, static arguments get their kinds. Everything inside white brackets
139	parses as a *type* argument — the comment in the code says so, "All Args are
140	parsed as TypeArgs" (`compiler/disambiguator/TypeDisambiguator.java:663-665`) —
141	and the disambiguator looks each one up and rewrites it: if the parameter it
142	names was declared `nat` or `int`, the `TypeArg(VarType k)` becomes
143	`IntArg(IntRef k)` (`TypeDisambiguator.java:667-697`, the `forKindNat` case at
144	`:694-697`). This is why sizes reach the checker as a different kind of node
145	from types, and why they need their own treatment there (section 8).
146	
147	**GRAMMAR, and the two moments of user syntax.** A user-defined grammar is
148	compiled in two places at two times (`modules-and-phases.md` B.3). When the
149	*api* that declares the grammar is analysed, the GRAMMAR phase rewrites the
150	grammar declarations and parses the template bodies into AST fragments with
151	holes (`phases/GrammarPhase.java:40`,
152	`syntax_abstractions/phases/GrammarRewriter.java:72-125`). When a *component*
153	that imports such a grammar is read, a parser for that grammar is generated on
154	the spot — a full Rats! run plus a `javac` run in a fresh temporary directory —
155	the component is parsed with it, and the macro expander `Transform` replaces
156	every use of user syntax with ordinary AST (`compiler/Parser.java:111-135`,
157	`:259-281`; `syntax_abstractions/rats/RatsParserGenerator.java:53-66`;
158	`syntax_abstractions/phases/Transform.java:61`).
159	
160	The expansion happens in the repository, before any phase runs on the
161	component (`repository/GraphRepository.java:511`), so the GRAMMAR phase's
162	position in the phase array applies to apis only, and by phase 1 a program's
163	user syntax is already gone (`modules-and-phases.md` B.3).
164	
165	**PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR.** The last phase before the checker. It produces code
166	that must itself be checked: comprehensions and big operators become
167	`__generate`/`__bigOperator` calls against the library's reduction objects,
168	generator lists become `loop` chains, generalized `if`/`while` become
169	`__cond`/`__whileCond`
170	(`desugarer/PreTypeCheckDesugaringVisitor.java:142-165, 245, 301, 333-335`).
171	
172	**INTEGERLITERALFOLDING** follows, on the compile path only
173	(`phases/PhaseOrder.java:142`): integer-literal expressions are folded to
174	atoms.
175	
176	**What is written to disk in between.** Analysis results are serialized as
177	text — a parenthesized dump of the tree — into `default_repository/caches/`:
178	`.tfi` for an api, `.tfs` for a component
179	(`nodes_util/ASTIO.java:92-120`; `repository/ProjectProperties.java:319, 323`).
180	Two facts about that cache decide a lot of debugging. The file name is the api
181	name plus a hash **of the source directory path, not of the content**
182	(`compiler/NamingCzar.java:244-254`), and staleness is decided by file dates
183	alone (`modules-and-phases.md` B.10). So a cache written under one prelude
184	poisons the other, and an edit that does not move a date is invisible; the
185	standing advice is to wipe (`repo-internals.md:152-160`).
186

582	## 7. Native bindings in both worlds
583	
584	The two paths bind Java code by two mechanisms that share nothing but the word
585	"native" (`modules-and-phases.md` B.12).
586	
587	**The interpreter: `builtinPrimitive`.** A function whose body is literally
588	`builtinPrimitive("some.java.Class")` is pattern-matched by
589	`NativeApp.checkAndLoadNative` (`interpreter/glue/NativeApp.java:157-215`,
590	the test at `:188`), and that class — a subclass of `NativeFn0..3` or
591	`NativeMeth0..3` under `interpreter/glue/` — is loaded reflectively and takes
592	the evaluator's boxed values directly. There are 231 such bindings in
593	`LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`, 108 in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and
594	7 in `LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss`; 427 across the whole interpreter world
595	(`modules-and-phases.md` B.12; `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md`, quoted in
596	FACTS).
597	
598	**The compile path: `import java`.** A `.fss` writes

602	synthesizes a Fortress api for it
603	(`repository/ForeignJava.java:132-136, 565-575`), and `FortressTransformer`
604	rewrites the class into a wrapper whose methods take and return the compiled
605	world's boxed values, written into `nativewrapper_cache`
606	(`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressTransformer.java:33, 37`). The helpers
607	themselves are plain static Java methods: `nativeHelpers/`, 24 classes,
608	2,377 lines (`modules-and-phases.md` A.2).

611	path: `ForeignComponentWrapper` populates an environment from `ForeignJava`'s

46

54	
55	The gate is strong where the 2012 team spent its last two years (codegen, the compiler front end, diagnostics) and blind where the team stopped: the bytecode optimizer (zero tests), syntax abstraction (one file), the cache round trip (not asserted), concurrency (every shard runs one thread), the linker, the unparser (`test-coverage.md` C.3).
